synopsis: The corpus treats the seven-day Caterpillar 793B radar-warning field test at a US copper mine in 2004, published by NIOSH in 2006, as its strongest available quantitative alarm-performance evidence [f11774, f5173]. Testing covered normal loading, hauling, dumping, parking and maintenance manoeuvres; 580 alarms sounded over 618 reversals, approximately 94% of reverse movements [f3269, f14431, f3010]. Of those alarms, 102 (18%) were false and 243 (42%) were nuisance alarms, leaving 235 warranting action or extra caution; the corpus reports that last share as either 40% or 41%, explicitly attributing the difference to rounding [f5174, f5175, f3277]. No missed detections were reported, but the audible warning was found disabled after shifts, so detection performance did not ensure continued use of the audible warning [f3278, f11780]. False alarms arose from ruts, rocks, foliage and the truck’s own rear tires, while nuisance alarms included real objects already known to the driver [f11779, f7002]. Chapter 9 also describes a Preco Preview trial at Phelps Dodge Morenci whose occasional false alarms were reportedly insufficient to cause the system to be ignored; the glossary calls this another trial, so its more favorable account should not automatically be merged with the disabled-alarm finding [f7001, f14434, f104].
